texts.preamble: State Of Gujarat vs Shaikh Adambhai Mahammadbhai on 4 March, 2022
texts.facts: Present appeal is filed by the appellant- original complainant challenging the impugned judgment and order rendered in Criminal Appeal No.38 of 2002 by the Additional Sessions Judge, Fast Track Court No.8, Nadiad dated 23.01.2007 recording acquittal of the respondent accused for the offence under Section 2(1-a), 2(a)(b), 2(a)(c) and 2(1-a)(m) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, on the grounds stated in the memo of appeal. 2. Though served, nobody appears for Respondent- original accused. 3. The brief facts of the prosecution case is that when the complainant who was serving as Food Inspector, Nadiad, visited the shop of the accused at Talav Darwaja, Balasinor. By giving identification and for analysis, the complainant purchased 600 gms besan for Rs.10.80/-. Thereafter, the complainant seized the said sample in the three bottles and packed the besan in bottles and thereafter, he sealed those bottles airtight and sent the same to the Public Analyst, Rajkot through S. T. parcel and other two bottles were sent to the Local Health Authority, Naidad. In the report of PUBLIC Analyst, it was reported that the said besan was misbranded and hence, he obtained the permission from the Local Health Authority as per the law to lodge complaint against the accused/ respondent on 24.08.1995 before the Judicial R/CR.A/252/2008 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/03/2022 Magistrate First Class, Balasinor. Thereafter, the case was registered and investigation is completed. By order dated 29.06.2002, the Judicial Magistrate First Class has convicted the respondent- accused in Criminal Case No.399 of 1995. Being aggrieved by the said order of conviction, the respondent-accused has filed criminal appeal before the Additional Sessions Court, Fast Track Court, Nadiad. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order of acquittal, the appellant has preferred the present appeal.
texts.arguments: 4. Mr. Devnani, learned APP for the appellant- original complainant referred to the papers and submitted that whether the acquittal could have been recorded for the reasons or the grounds mentioned, is required to be considered. He emphasized that the observations have been made that the panch-witness has not supported the case of the prosecution on the extent of variety of besan sample. He submitted that the approach cannot be so casual. He referred to the testimony of the Food Inspector. He submitted that the manner in which, the sample has been taken, is also stated and he has narrated about the entire procedure. He therefore submitted that it cannot be said that the provisions of law and mandatory provisions are not complied with. He has also referred to the judgment recording the reasons for the findings and conclusion arrived at by the Court below and R/CR.A/252/2008 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/03/2022 submitted that the reasons recorded are contrary to the material and it has failed to appreciate the evidence on record. Mr. Devnani strenuously submitted that contradictions or the discrepancies must be shown to have caused prejudice or they have affected the root of the matter. He submitted that unless it is shown that the State Of Gujarat vs Shaikh Adambhai Mahammadbhai on 4 March, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/60866115/ 2 prejudice is caused, the benefit of doubt would not be justified. Learned APP Mr.Devnani submitted that the documents which have been relevant and the documents which the accused was carrying were required. Therefore, he would not make any evidence. He submitted that sampling was followed on the other occasion also. He submitted that the act prescribes procedure and the law and therefore, it has to be construed strictly. The Hon'ble Apex Court in catena of judicial pronouncements has laid down the broad guidelines with regard to scope of Section 378 and approach in such acquittal R/CR.A/252/2008 JUDGMENT DATED: 04/03/2022 appeals including the observations made in a judgment reported in (2007) 4 SCC 415 in the case of Chandrappa and Ors., Vs. State of Karnataka., wherein it has been observed that, "42. From the above decisions, in our considered view, the following general principles regarding powers of the appellate Court while dealing with an appeal against an order of acquittal emerge; [1] An appellate Court has full power to review, re-appreciate and reconsider the evidence upon which the order of acquittal is founded. [2] The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 puts no limitation, restriction or condition on exercise of such power and an appellate Court on the evidence before it may reach its own conclusion, both on questions of fact and of law. [ 3 ] Various expressions, such as, "substantial and compelling reasons", "good and sufficient grounds", "very strong circumstances", "distorted conclusions", "glaring mistakes", etc. are not intended to curtain extensive powers of an appellate Court in an appeal against acquittal. Such phraseologies are more in the nature of "flourishes of language" to emphasis the reluctance of an appellate Court to interfere with acquittal than to curtail the power of the Court to review the evidence and to come to its own conclusion. Firstly, the presumption of innocence is available to him under the fundamental principle of criminal jurisprudence that every person shall be presumed to be innocent unless he is proved guilty by a competent Court of law. [5] If two reasonable conclusions are possible on the basis of the evidence on record, the appellate Court should not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded by the trial Court." Further, the same view has also been reiterated and reconsidered again in a subsequent judgment including observations made in a judgment reported in a judgment reported in AIR 2013 SC 321 in the case of Mookiiah and Anr. Vs. State, represented by the Inspector of Police, Tamil Nadu. Again emphasizing that if the view taken by the Court below is plausible view the same may not be disturbed, merely because the other view is also possible on appreciation of the same evidence. Further, while discussing on this aspect about the approach, a reference can be made to another judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court reported in 2011 (5) SCC 142 in the case of Chiarman-cum-Managing Director, Coal Indian Limited and Ors., Vs. Ananta Saha and Others.
